objections.title: 1. “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”
objections.whoRaises: Hume, Russell, Hospers, Dawkins, Dennett, Harris, Hitchens, Krauss — the single most common objection
objections.objection: The cosmological argument says everything needs a cause. Then God needs one too. If you exempt God, you are special pleading — and if God can be uncaused, so can the universe.
objections.reply:
1. None of the five proofs has the premise ‘everything has a cause’. The principles are narrower: whatever goes from potential to actual (ch. 1), whatever is composite (ch. 2), whatever has an essence distinct from its existence (ch. 4), or whatever is contingent (ch. 5) needs a cause.
2. The exemption for God is not arbitrary; it is the *conclusion*. Each proof identifies the feature that makes things need a cause and shows there must be something that lacks that very feature — pure actuality, simplicity, essence identical with existence, necessity.
3. So the question becomes ‘What actualized the potentials of that which has no potentials?’ or ‘What combined the parts of that which has no parts?’ — which makes no sense.
4. Against the rationalist proof it is weaker still: PSR says *everything* has an explanation, God included; his is found in his own nature.
5. The Augustinian proof is not a causal argument, so the objection does not even touch it.
objections.pushback: If the critic says the distinction is an ad hoc dodge, note (ch. 1) that motives are irrelevant to soundness (ad hominem), that the ‘potential to actual’ formulation has been the claim for over two millennia, and that it follows from the analysis of change independently of theology. If he asks where the ‘everything has a cause’ version comes from, chapter 7 traces it, following W. Norris Clarke, through Russell and the Mills to Hume’s conflation of ‘cause’ with ‘sufficient reason’ in Descartes and Spinoza — and not one major defender of the argument ever used it. Then invite him to say which premise of an actual proof he rejects.

objections.title: 2. “The argument assumes the universe had a beginning”
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic; Rosenberg and Krauss (multiverse); many textbook summaries
objections.objection: Cosmology is unsettled. Maybe there was no Big Bang ‘first moment’ — an eternal universe, an oscillating cosmos, or a beginningless multiverse. Then there is no first event for God to cause.
objections.reply:
1. The four causal proofs grant, for the sake of argument, a beginningless universe or multiverse (ch. 1, 2, 4, 5). Aristotle himself thought the world had no beginning.
2. The concern is not what started things but what **sustains** them at every moment: the concurrent actualization of the coffee’s existence (ch. 1), the concurrent combination of the chair’s parts (ch. 2), the imparting of existence to Fido here and now (ch. 4), the persistence of any contingent thing now (ch. 5).
3. Such dependence forms a hierarchical series, which needs an underived first member however long the universe has existed.
4. Only the kalām cosmological argument (not defended in the book) tries to prove a beginning.
objections.pushback: If the critic insists that ‘first cause’ must mean first in time, show the paintbrush: an infinitely long handle still needs a hand. If he says every present state is explained by the previous state, distinguish explaining how something *got here* from explaining what keeps it *existing now* (ch. 1’s water example; ch. 4’s Fido). Chapter 7 repeats the point against the multiverse.

objections.title: 3. “Why can’t an infinite regress do all the explaining?”
objections.whoRaises: Hume (Dialogues); Graham Oppy; Krauss (endless layers of laws)
objections.objection: If each member of a causal series is explained by the one before it, every member is explained. An infinite series leaves nothing unexplained, so no first cause is needed. Mathematics is full of infinite series; why not causes?
objections.reply:
1. For **linear** series Feser agrees: they may in principle be infinite (ch. 1).
2. But in a **hierarchical** series every member other than the first has only borrowed power. Adding more borrowers never produces a lender. Infinite mirrors still need a face; infinite IOUs never become money; an infinitely long brush handle cannot move itself (ch. 1, 4, 7).
3. Barry Miller’s point (ch. 4): the explanation has the form ‘A is caused by B inasmuch as B is caused by C inasmuch as …’, and the sentence can only be completed by naming a first member.
4. Mathematical infinite series involve no instrumental causation at all, so they are not counterexamples (ch. 1).
5. For the rationalist proof, the whole series still needs explaining (why it exists, why this content — Leibniz’s geometry books), and explaining it by further contingent causes only creates a higher-order series with the same problem (ch. 5).
objections.pushback: If the critic says calling the intermediate causes ‘instrumental’ begs the question (Jordan Howard Sobel), reply (ch. 1) that ‘instrumental’ just means ‘deriving its power from something else’ — anyone can see a stick has no power of its own to push a stone — and nothing in that description presupposes that the regress terminates. For Krauss’s layers of laws, note that levels of laws form exactly such a hierarchy (ch. 7).

objections.title: 4. “First-cause arguments commit the fallacy of composition”
objections.whoRaises: Hume, Russell, A. C. Grayling
objections.objection: Each brick may weigh a pound without the wall weighing a pound. Likewise, each thing in the universe may need a cause without the universe as a whole needing one.
objections.reply:
1. Most of the proofs make no claim about the universe as a whole as a premise; they start from one thing — a cup of coffee, Fido, a stone. That God causes everything is a conclusion (ch. 1, 4, 7).
2. Not all part-to-whole reasoning is fallacious: if every Lego block is red, the wall is red. It depends on the property (ch. 4, 5).
3. Contingency behaves like color, not weight: a collection of contingent things is if anything *more* contingent — dependent on its members and on their being assembled (ch. 5).
4. In fact the critic commits the fallacy: from ‘each stick’s motion is explained by the next stick’ it does not follow that the motion in the whole series is explained (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If he replies that the ‘universe’ is not a thing but just a label for its members, then there is nothing extra to explain away — and the proofs, which start from any single contingent thing’s existence here and now (ch. 5’s second route), go through anyway.

objections.title: 5. “Hume showed something could come into being without a cause”
objections.whoRaises: Hume; Grayling; many analytic philosophers
objections.objection: I can conceive of a coffee cup suddenly appearing out of nothing, with no cause. What is conceivable is possible. So the principle of causality is not necessarily true.
objections.reply:
1. Conceiving of A *without conceiving of* B is not conceiving of A *existing without* B. I can conceive of a trilateral without thinking ‘triangle’, or of a man without thinking of his height; it does not follow that either could exist without the other (ch. 1, 7).
2. Elizabeth Anscombe’s point: what makes the imagined scenario a case of *coming into being* rather than being teleported from elsewhere? Only reference to the kind of cause — which brings causation back in (ch. 1, 7).
3. Empirically, the principle is as well confirmed as anything: we find causes when we look, and hotels and elephants do not pop onto our lawns (W. Norris Clarke) (ch. 1).
4. As Gerson notes, ‘maybe there is no explanation’ is not an alternative to an explanation that has been given (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic retreats to Kant — the principle may hold within experience but cannot be applied beyond it — reply that we affirm causes not because things are experienced but because they are potential until actualized, a completely general truth; compare Euclidean geometry, learned from black ink drawings but true of figures of any color (ch. 1).

objections.title: 6. “Quantum mechanics shows events without causes”
objections.whoRaises: Stenger, Dennett, Rosenberg; popular science writing
objections.objection: Radioactive decay and vacuum fluctuations happen at random. Physics has discovered genuinely uncaused events, so the principle of causality and PSR are false.
objections.reply:
1. Causation does not require determinism; a cause need only make its effect intelligible (ch. 1). On standard interpretations every quantum transition has causal antecedents (Koons).
2. A Pb-210 atom decays with a certain probability because of what it is — its nature is a formal cause — and something generated it and keeps it existing now; Phil Dowe notes physicists speak of decay ‘producing’ mercury (ch. 1).
3. Physics is a mathematical abstraction that by method leaves out potentiality and causation; the absence of a cause in the representation is not a representation of its absence — like the lack of color in a line drawing (ch. 1).
4. Quantum events occur only given the laws of quantum mechanics and a universe that follows them, which are themselves what needs explaining (ch. 5, 7). Chance presupposes non-chance regularities — the farmer who finds buried treasure (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If pressed on Bell correlations or particles appearing in a vacuum, note the variety of available interpretations, but return to the deeper point: interpretation of quantum theory cannot decide a metaphysical question it methodologically brackets. Heisenberg himself compared quantum states to Aristotle’s *potentia* (ch. 1).

objections.title: 7. “Modern physics has eliminated causation and change”
objections.whoRaises: Early Russell (‘On the Notion of Cause’); appeals to Newton’s law of inertia, Einstein’s block universe, Eddington’s ‘two tables’
objections.objection: Physics describes the world with equations, not causes. Inertia shows motion needs no mover; relativity suggests past and future are as real as the present, so nothing really changes; and physics tells us the table is a cloud of particles, not a solid thing holding up a cup.
objections.reply:
1. Russell’s argument proves too much: ‘law’, ‘event’ and ‘explanation’ are not in the equations either (Schaffer). Particles have dispositions (C. B. Martin), other sciences use causal notions, and naturalists rely on causal theories of perception and meaning (ch. 1).
2. Physics captures only mathematically describable structure; the later Russell admitted it is silent about the intrinsic nature of what changes (ch. 1, 7).
3. Newton’s law presupposes the existence of the bodies it describes, so it cannot explain their existence; and on an Aristotelian reading a law describes how a thing behaves given its nature (ch. 1).
4. Even if the block universe were true, the experiences on which physics rests involve change (Richard Healey), and the sheer existence of such a universe would still need an actualizer (ch. 1).
5. The particle picture merely supplies the mechanism by which the desk holds up the cup; the examples only introduce act/potency and hierarchical series, which apply at any level (ch. 1).
objections.pushback: If the critic says Aristotelianism in general was refuted by modern science, separate the outdated physics (geocentrism, natural places) from the metaphysical thesis that change is actualization of potential, which science presupposes rather than refutes (ch. 1). If he insists simultaneity of cause and effect is impossible, note that ‘simultaneous’ does not mean ‘instantaneous’, and the immediate cause and effect are one event (Mumford and Anjum) (ch. 1).

objections.title: 8. “Maybe the universe itself (or the laws, the Big Bang, the multiverse) is the necessary, uncaused thing”
objections.whoRaises: Hume; Dawkins, Dennett, Grayling, Krauss, Rosenberg, Stenger
objections.objection: Grant that explanation must stop somewhere. Why stop at God? Stop at the universe, or at the laws of physics, and you have saved a step.
objections.reply:
1. The stopping point is principled. What ends the regress must be purely actual, simple, identical with its own existence and necessary (ch. 5, 6, 7).
2. The universe changes (so it has potency), has parts (so it is composite), and is contingent; so do the Big Bang, each stage of a multiverse and each quantum event (ch. 5, 7).
3. Laws cannot be ultimate on any account of them: as mere descriptions of regularities they explain nothing; as Platonic entities we would need to explain why the world participates in these rather than others; as descriptions of how natures behave they presuppose the things that have the natures (ch. 7).
4. If the universe really were necessary, uncaused and self-explanatory, it would have divine attributes — the result would be pantheism, not atheism (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic replies with Kant that a necessary being presupposes the ontological argument, answer (ch. 7) that God’s necessity is not ‘existence by definition’ but the metaphysical necessity of what is purely actual, simple and self-existent; Aquinas rejects the ontological argument while accepting the cosmological. And Grayling’s dilemma (logical vs. merely conditional necessity) is a false one. If the critic appeals to numbers as non-divine necessary beings, chapter 3 argues they cannot exist apart from a mind (ch. 5, note).

objections.title: 9. “PSR is false — reality can end in brute facts”
objections.whoRaises: J. L. Mackie, Bertrand Russell; van Inwagen, Rowe (the big conjunctive contingent fact)
objections.objection: We can explain phenomena by laws and those by deeper laws, but the deepest laws are simply there. Besides, PSR leads to paradox: the conjunction of all contingent truths can be explained neither by a necessary truth (which entails only necessary truths) nor by a contingent one (which would be part of what needs explaining).
objections.reply:
1. Denying PSR undercuts perception (Pruss, Koons) and even the rational grounds of one’s own beliefs, including disbelief in PSR (ch. 5).
2. A regress of laws ending in a brute fact makes every explanation illusory: a book on a shelf that stays up for no reason has not been explained — the brackets cannot be let go in mid-air (ch. 5, 7).
3. Della Rocca: critics use explicability arguments everywhere else and have no non-question-begging reason to exempt existence (ch. 5).
4. The big-conjunction puzzle assumes propositions are Platonic objects needing explanation and that explanation requires entailment. For a Scholastic realist, once concrete things and the minds that entertain propositions are explained, nothing is left over; and scientific explanations do not entail their explananda (ch. 5).
5. Brute-fact appeals are ad hoc, adopted only to avoid theism (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘maybe there’s just no explanation’, answer with Gerson: an explanation has been given; to reject it you must show what is wrong with it (ch. 2, 7). If he demands that PSR be proved directly, explain that it is known indirectly, by *reductio*, because it is more evident than any premise for or against it (ch. 5).

objections.title: 10. “Even if there’s a first cause, it needn’t be God”
objections.whoRaises: Dawkins, Grayling (‘the usual big jump’), Krauss; a staple of popular criticism
objections.objection: At best you get some cause of the universe — perhaps impersonal, perhaps finite, perhaps one of many. Nothing licenses omnipotence, omniscience, goodness or unity.
objections.reply:
1. Every chapter’s Stage 2 derives the attributes from the Stage 1 description: pure actuality yields immutability, eternity, immateriality, perfection, goodness, omnipotence; the PPC yields intellect and omniscience; the impossibility of differentiating purely actual beings yields uniqueness (ch. 1–5).
2. Chapter 6 develops each attribute at length and shows the five routes reach the same being.
3. Historically, proponents always argued for the attributes — Aquinas devoted a vast stretch of the *Summa* to them, and Samuel Clarke’s book is largely about them (ch. 7).
4. The objection is usually made in ignorance that these arguments exist.
objections.pushback: If the critic says a first cause could have potentials that are simply not being exercised, answer (ch. 1) that a first actualizer of existence with unactualized potential would need something further to actualize it, so it would not be first; a partly potential ‘first cause’ collapses into a regress. If he says ‘impersonal’, point to intellect via the PPC and chapter 3, and to will and love in chapter 6.

objections.title: 11. “A thing’s parts might unify themselves”
objections.whoRaises: Critic of the Neo-Platonic proof (considered by Vallicella and Gerson)
objections.objection: Why assume an external cause must combine a composite’s parts? Perhaps one of its parts does the unifying, or its unity is an irreducible fact, or laws of nature explain it.
objections.reply:
1. If part C unifies parts A and B, what unites C with them? Positing D just repeats the problem; the regress compounds rather than solves it (ch. 2).
2. ‘Irreducible fact’ means either the composite causes its own unity — which makes it both cause and effect of its composition, incoherent — or its unity has no cause at all, which is not an alternative explanation but the absence of one (ch. 2).
3. Laws of nature plus the things they govern form a further composite whose composition needs explaining; and on the Aristotelian view laws presuppose the combination of form and matter (ch. 2).
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘fine, there is no explanation’, repeat Gerson’s response: an explanation has been offered, and one needs a non-question-begging reason to reject it (ch. 2). Note also that for the rationalist proof the same demand follows from PSR (ch. 5).

objections.title: 12. “The essence/existence distinction is merely conceptual”
objections.whoRaises: Anthony Kenny; analytic critics appealing to Frege’s quantifier view and to intensional contexts
objections.objection: That I can know what a lion is without knowing whether lions exist shows only that the concept of a lion differs from the concept of its existence — just as I can know aspirin relieves pain without knowing that acetylsalicylic acid does. And existence is just the quantifier ‘there is an x such that…’, not something a thing has.
objections.reply:
1. Klima: substitution fails in intentional contexts only when the concepts are logically independent. A *complete* grasp of aspirin’s chemistry would include its being acetylsalicylic acid; no complete grasp of a lion’s essence ever includes its existence (ch. 4).
2. Judging that lions do not exist is judging falsely, not misconceiving what a lion is — unlike judging a lion is not a cat (ch. 4).
3. Contingency and plurality give independent grounds: things could fail to exist, and there can be many of a kind (ch. 4).
4. Kenny assumes a real distinction requires separability (radius and circumference refute that) and that quantifier-existence is the only respectable notion. But ‘there is an x that is a cat’ leaves open what makes it true that something falls under the concept — which is precisely existence as act (Knasas, Klima) (ch. 4).
objections.pushback: If the critic doubts that things have real essences at all, point to the unity of natural kinds and individuals, the practice of physics looking for natures under controlled conditions (Cartwright), the discrete kinds of chemistry (Ellis), and Crawford Elder’s argument that conventionalism about all essences — including the mind’s — is incoherent (ch. 4).

objections.title: 13. “Abstract objects don’t need a divine mind”
objections.whoRaises: Platonists; nominalists and conceptualists; Yandell and Craig (divine ideas aren’t abstract); Brian Leftow; Patrick Grim
objections.objection: Either abstract objects are Platonic entities existing necessarily in no mind, or they are human constructs. Ideas in God would be concrete mental items, not abstract objects. And omniscience is incoherent anyway — Cantor’s theorem shows there is no set of all truths.
objections.reply:
1. Nominalism and conceptualism are self-undermining (resemblance regress; words are universals; shared meaning and communication; psychologism refutes itself) (ch. 3).
2. Platonic objects would be causally inert and unknowable, and a Form would have to be both universal and an individual — animality itself neither rational nor nonrational (ch. 3).
3. The ‘not really abstract’ objection begs the question: for Aristotelians and Scholastics an abstract object *is* what an intellect forms by abstracting; there is no consensus notion that settles the matter against them (Welty) (ch. 3).
4. Grim’s argument proves too much — there would be no set of all propositions, yet we truly say all propositions are true or false (Plantinga); omniscience needs only that there is no truth God fails to know (Simmons); and simplicity means God’s knowledge is not a set of discrete ideas (Wainwright) (ch. 3).
5. Leftow’s worry that God would ‘depend’ on water being H₂O is no worse than arithmetic ‘depending’ on rocks (ch. 3).
objections.pushback: If the critic, like Coffey, says we cannot know possibilities are eternal without first knowing God, note that even atheist Platonists affirm eternal possibilities; the argument simply denies they can be housed in a third realm (ch. 3). Welty’s relevance condition helps too: a Platonic possible world, like a drawing, cannot make it true that Socrates could have been a carpenter; an idea in an omnipotent mind can.

objections.title: 14. “Divine simplicity is incoherent”
objections.whoRaises: Alvin Plantinga; Thomas Morris; theistic personalists
objections.objection: If God is identical with each of his properties, then all his properties are identical — power is mercy — and God himself is a property, a mere abstract object. Also, some truths about God are necessary (he is omnipotent) and some contingent (he created this world), so they cannot all be one.
objections.reply:
1. Plantinga reads the doctrine through his own assumptions: a very broad notion of ‘property’, properties as Platonic abstracta, and univocal predication. Classical theists reject all three (ch. 6).
2. Distinguish essence, properties (in the Thomist sense), accidents and relations; these are constituents of a thing, not Platonic entities (ch. 6).
3. God’s power and knowledge differ in sense but are one reality, as with the morning and evening star; we speak of them analogically (ch. 2, 6).
4. Morris’s point is met by Geach’s and Miller’s ‘Cambridge properties’: God’s having created the world is a Cambridge property, involving a real change only in the world; simplicity identifies only God’s real properties (ch. 6).
5. Without simplicity God would need a cause and could have rivals — a superangel, not God (ch. 6).
objections.pushback: If the critic says theism can do without simplicity, reply that the causal proofs are ipso facto proofs of a simple cause; deny simplicity and you deny what the proofs reach, and even the uniqueness of God becomes a contingent fact (ch. 6). Dawkins’ ‘God would be complex’ is the same mistake from the atheist side (ch. 7).

objections.title: 15. “An immutable, timeless God couldn’t create, act, know, love or choose freely”
objections.whoRaises: Swinburne, Pike (timelessness); Kretzmann, Rowe (freedom); process theists (love)
objections.objection: Acting changes the agent; creating is a transition from not-creating to creating; causing things at different times puts God in time; love means being affected; free choice means actualizing one potential rather than another; and a perfectly good God would have to create the best possible world, so he isn’t free.
objections.reply:
1. That agents in our experience change when they act is a **fallacy of accident** if taken as essential; what is essential to acting is producing an effect (Brian Davies) (ch. 1, 6).
2. Becoming Creator is a Cambridge change (ch. 6).
3. From ‘God causes X to exist at t1’ it does not follow that ‘at t1 God causes X’; God causes a whole temporal world in one act, like an author conceiving a story (ch. 6). Eternity is not a point in time that could be simultaneous with Socrates and with Obama.
4. Love is essentially willing the good of another, not emotion; God wills creatures’ good in creating them (ch. 6).
5. Freedom needs no passive potency, only the absence of compulsion from within or without; there is no obligation to create, and there is no best possible world, since for any world with x forests there is one with x + 1 (ch. 6).
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘I can’t understand free choice without potency’, concede that it is hard to grasp positively — Davies suggests reading it partly as negative theology — and note that difficulty is expected when reasoning reaches the ultimate level of reality, just as with wave-particle duality (ch. 2, 6). If he argues that God would be more perfect by creating a better world, answer that God’s perfection follows from what he is, not what he makes, like a perfect diamond whether or not it cuts glass (ch. 6).

objections.title: 16. “If God knows the future, we aren’t free”
objections.whoRaises: Nelson Pike; a very common lay worry
objections.objection: If God infallibly knows I will go to work tomorrow, I cannot fail to go; and since God knows by causing, he causes my choices. Either way my freedom is an illusion.
objections.reply:
1. Knowledge of an action, however certain, does not cause it: my knowing you sit in the next room doesn’t make your sitting unfree, and the same holds if I somehow know it in advance (ch. 6).
2. God is the cause of the world as an author is the cause of a story, not as a hypnotist inside the story; a character can freely commit a crime in a novel the author wrote (ch. 6).
3. Because God is outside time, he does not ‘foreknow’ by peering ahead; he knows the whole world by knowing himself as its cause (ch. 6).
4. Concurrence: like a child whose hand is guided by a parent teaching him to write, our free choice makes a real contribution even though nothing happens without God’s action (ch. 6).
objections.pushback: If the critic says the author analogy works only because characters are fictional, reply that the point concerns the *logical kind* of relation — primary cause of the whole versus one cause among others — and that treating God’s causality univocally with creaturely causality is exactly the error analogy avoids (ch. 6).

objections.title: 17. “It’s a god of the gaps — science will explain it (it already has: a universe from nothing)”
objections.whoRaises: Hitchens, Dawkins, Harris; Krauss; Hawking and Mlodinow
objections.objection: God is posited to fill a gap in scientific knowledge. Parsimony says prefer a physical explanation; indeed physics shows the universe can arise from nothing thanks to laws like gravity.
objections.reply:
1. The proofs are not gap-fillers or probabilistic hypotheses but demonstrations claiming no non-divine explanation is possible in principle (ch. 7).
2. Their starting points — change, composition, essence-existence, contingency — are presupposed by any empirical theory, so no empirical discovery could remove them (ch. 7).
3. Hawking and Mlodinow’s ‘law like gravity’ is not nothing; Krauss’s candidates (empty space with energy, quantum laws, layers of laws) are admittedly not nothing either, as the philosopher of physics David Albert pointed out (ch. 7).
4. Nothing is not an exotic stuff; it is the absence of anything.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘we don’t yet know how the universe began’, remind him the proofs do not depend on how or whether it began (ch. 1, 7). If he says only scientific explanations count, move to objection 18.

objections.title: 18. “Science is the only genuine source of knowledge”
objections.whoRaises: Alex Rosenberg; New Atheists generally (scientism)
objections.objection: Physics’ predictive and technological success shows its methods are the right ones for all knowledge. Metaphysics produces no technology and no consensus. Natural theology isn’t science, so it isn’t knowledge.
objections.reply:
1. Dilemma: the claim ‘only science gives knowledge’ is not itself a scientific result, so it is self-refuting; if ‘science’ is stretched to include philosophy, the claim becomes trivial and natural theology could count as science too (ch. 7).
2. Physics abstracts from everything unquantifiable, so it cannot in principle give a complete description of reality — as Russell admitted, it gives structure, not intrinsic nature (ch. 1, 7).
3. Laws cannot provide ultimate explanation on any theory of what laws are (ch. 7).
4. The success argument is like inferring from metal detectors’ success that only metal exists, or from straight A’s in easy classes that other subjects aren’t worth studying (ch. 7).
5. The science/conceptual-analysis dichotomy is a version of Hume’s fork, which refutes itself; logic and mathematics fit neither prong (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘fine, but philosophy never settles anything’, reply that insisting only consensus-yielding questions matter is itself a philosophical claim needing philosophical defense, and that restricting ‘science’ to what is predictable guarantees trivially that science is a success story (ch. 7).

objections.title: 19. “Evil (and God’s hiddenness) shows there is no good God”
objections.whoRaises: J. L. Mackie (logical), William Rowe (evidential — the fawn), J. L. Schellenberg (hiddenness)
objections.objection: An omnipotent, perfectly good God would eliminate evil — or at least pointless suffering like a fawn burning slowly in a forest fire. And a loving God would make his existence obvious. Neither is the case.
objections.reply:
1. Mackie’s premises fail: omnipotence does not include doing contradictions, and a good being need not eliminate every evil if that would eliminate goods logically requiring it — forgiveness and mercy require wrongdoing; courage requires danger; compassion requires suffering (ch. 7). Mackie himself later conceded the logical argument fails.
2. Evil is privation, not a positive thing God must contain (ch. 6).
3. Rowe’s argument is only as strong as the claim that no greater good is served; anyone with independent demonstrations of a good, omnipotent God has reason to believe there is one, even when we cannot say what it is (ch. 7).
4. An afterlife, which is at least possible, could outweigh all earthly evils, as adulthood makes sense of childhood’s trials (ch. 7).
5. Hiddenness: not all theists hold that God seeks a personal relationship (Aristotle’s God), and most humans have in fact believed in the divine; the ‘epistemic distance’ that exists stems from finite minds and free will (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic says this is cold comfort to sufferers, agree that a *defense* (showing consistency) is not a *theodicy* (explaining specific evils) and not pastoral care — Feser explicitly offers only a defense (ch. 7). If he asks why we should expect to be ignorant of God’s reasons, point to the child-adult analogy and to the incomprehensibility of God (ch. 6, 7).

objections.title: 20. “Go one god further” / “That’s not the God people actually worship”
objections.whoRaises: Dawkins, Colin McGinn; critics who contrast the ‘God of the philosophers’ with the God of religion
objections.objection: You reject Zeus, Thor and Quetzalcoatl; atheists just reject one more god. And the abstract ‘ground of being’ of the proofs is not the personal God ordinary believers pray to.
objections.reply:
1. There are demonstrations for classical theism’s God and none for Zeus (ch. 7).
2. More deeply, it is a category mistake: classical theism’s God is not a member of a genus ‘gods’ (he would then have parts — genus and difference), not ‘a being’ among beings, but subsistent being itself. Comparing him to Zeus is like treating triangularity as one more, better-drawn triangle, or the Form of the Good as one more good thing (ch. 6, 7).
3. On the ‘God of the philosophers’: even if true it would be irrelevant — atheism would still be false. And it is false: Catholic teaching, for example, holds that the God known by reason and by revelation is the same; ordinary believers hold the same God in a less sophisticated way, as laymen believe in atoms without the physicist’s understanding (ch. 7).
objections.pushback: If the critic says the classical God is too abstract to be personal, point out that classical theists attribute intellect, will and love to God (ch. 6) — they deny only that personhood makes God one member of a genus. If he raises a specific religion’s claims, note that natural theology deliberately stops short of revealed religion; miracles would be the bridge (ch. 6).

misconceptions.myth: The proofs argue that the universe had a beginning and that God lit the fuse of the Big Bang.
misconceptions.correction: All four causal proofs grant a beginningless universe or multiverse for argument’s sake; they concern what sustains things in existence here and now through hierarchical causal series. Only the kalām argument, not defended in the book, tries to show a beginning.

misconceptions.myth: The proofs rest on the premise that everything has a cause.
misconceptions.correction: They rest on narrower principles — whatever goes from potential to actual, is composite, has essence distinct from existence, or is contingent needs a cause — and PSR, which says everything has an explanation (God’s lying in his own nature). No major defender of cosmological arguments ever used ‘everything has a cause’.

misconceptions.myth: The five proofs point to five different ultimate beings, or at best to a vague ‘first cause’.
misconceptions.correction: Chapter 6 shows that being purely actual, simple, subsistent existence and necessary entail one another, that a necessary intellect is purely actual, and that there can be only one such being. Every chapter’s Stage 2 derives the full set of divine attributes.

misconceptions.myth: They are scientific hypotheses — ‘God did it’ as a rival to physics, to be judged by parsimony and evidence.
misconceptions.correction: They are metaphysical demonstrations starting from what any scientific theory presupposes; they do not compete with physics at physics’ own level, and a scientific discovery could not overturn their premises.

misconceptions.myth: God, in these arguments, is the biggest and most powerful being in the universe — one item alongside others.
misconceptions.correction: God is not ‘a being’ within any genus but subsistent being itself, the source of the being and causal power of everything else. That is why ‘one god further’ and ‘who designed the designer?’ miss the target.

misconceptions.myth: Divine simplicity means God is simple-minded, has just one property, or is himself a property.
misconceptions.correction: Simplicity means God has no parts — no matter and form, genus and difference, essence distinct from existence, or really distinct attributes. His power, knowledge and goodness are one reality known under different descriptions, spoken of analogically.

misconceptions.myth: If language about God is analogical, it must be metaphorical or merely negative.
misconceptions.correction: Analogical predication is literal: ‘good’ in ‘good wine’ and ‘good man’ is neither identical nor unrelated. Much of our knowledge of God is negative, but analogy of attribution and of proper proportionality give real positive content.

misconceptions.myth: An immutable, timeless God would be inert, unfeeling and unable to act, know, choose or love.
misconceptions.correction: Being changed is not essential to acting, living, choosing or loving; to assume otherwise is a fallacy of accident. God acts without being acted upon, loves by willing the good of creatures, and is Creator by a Cambridge change in the world.

misconceptions.myth: Miracles would be violations of the laws of nature by a God who otherwise leaves the world to run on its own.
misconceptions.correction: God conserves and concurs with everything at every moment, so he cannot literally ‘intervene’. A miracle elevates a nature beyond its powers or suspends its operation by God’s refraining from conserving or concurring — more like a musician improvising than a mechanic forcing a machine.

misconceptions.myth: A real proof would convince every intelligent person who hears it; since many reject these, they aren’t proofs.
misconceptions.correction: A demonstration is a valid deduction from certain premises; it may require substantial work to understand and defend, and fair-minded people can fail to see its force. Controversy is not refutation — no one treats arguments for materialism that way.
